Wifi Analyzer app helps you identify optimal channels for your wireless router to improve speed
This is my first go to app when ever there is a problem with WiFi at work. Been using this app for a couple of years now, so much better than lugging around a laptop to analyze the signals!

Used it on a few different setups, interesting tool. The only problem I've had with it is that it doesn't remember intermittent connections, and the "star chart" never quite works.

Manual channel switching might save a millisecond or two if you're in a cardboard house with many active hotspots. I suppose it depends on the router but automatic channel selection isn't bad either, the problem with manual is that you're stuck with the one you choose. What works on Monday might not be best Saturday.

Most routers pick from 3 of the channels to attempt to prevent overlap. Once you have a few wireless signals in the same area auto is not the best option any more.

As was said in the previous comment this dose mean it will not automatically adapt if there is a new stronger signal interfering with yours.

Example
In your example it would be best to go to channels 3, 4, 8, or 9 as all other wireless networks on the area are the weakest at these frequencies (they are all concentrated at channels 1, 6, and 11).

If you use channels 2-5 you interfere with and get interference from 1 & 6, and 7-10 with/from 6 & 11.

You're better off choosing from 1/6/11 that is least congested, or best off moving up to 5ghz where there's way more non-overlapping channels.

Ok I see what you mean but looking at the graph you see the the interference at channel 3 for example is minimal from channel 1 and non existent from channel 6. It would look like channels 2, 5, 7, and 10 are the ones with the most interference. while 3, 4, 8, and 9 are the ones with the least.
Also, wouldn't a little interference be better than several overlapping signals on the same channel?

If would be more clear if they used a rectangle instead of an arc to represent the channels, because the strength of the signal is uniform not tapered off like that. 2.4Ghz ISM band channels (which existed WAY before wifi) are only 5Mhz apart, but wifi needs 20Mhz channels, the overlap is worse than it appears in that app.

Receivers (the important part with this) are better at dealing with another signal in the same channel than those that overlap from a different channel. Only use 1,6 & 11 (and 14 if applicable to your regulatory area). Many devices are smart enough to do this themselves, but there's entirely too many that will choose the "wrong" channels when set to auto.
